endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Develop a formal AI Policy document, approved by organizational leadership, and make accessible to all relevant staff.

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: Staff and providers should know where to gain access to relevant information about the AI tool and its use and what the organization’s AI policies and procedures are.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence in Psychiatric Graduate Medical Education
endorsements.issuer: Academic psychiatry : the journal of the American Association of Directors of Psychiatric Residency Training and the Association for Academic Psychiatry
endorsements.quote: Disseminate (or create, if not available) clear institutional guidelines delineating appropriate vs. Inappropriate AI use in educational contexts, with particular attention to maintaining academic integrity in curriculum design and assessment.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this recommendation tests whether plain-language summaries, role-specific materials, or recurring departmental communications raise staff awareness of AI policy or improve compliance. The recommendation rests on two endorsements, a CHAI playbook rated "must" and RUAIH guidance rated "should", which call for accessible policy and staff knowledge of where to find it.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, no certainty rating can be assigned to the effect of these dissemination methods. The two endorsements reflect expert consensus, and they carry no weight as effect estimates.

Both endorsing sources are voluntary framework and guidance documents rather than statutes or regulations. The CHAI text requires that an approved policy be accessible to relevant staff, and the RUAIH text asks that staff know where to find policies. Neither source specifies plain-language summaries, role-specific materials, or recurring departmental communications, so those specific methods go beyond what the endorsements state.

No supplied study measures how often staff are unaware of AI policy or whether that unawareness leads to unreported concerns or patient harm. The pathway from policy awareness to fewer errors reaching patients therefore remains a plausible assumption that the supplied evidence has not examined.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that measure baseline staff awareness of AI policy and compare dissemination methods, such as plain-language summaries, role-specific materials, and recurring departmental messages, against simple posting of the policy. Outcomes should include staff knowledge, policy compliance, and the rate at which staff report AI-related concerns.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Staff in safety-net settings, and staff whose first language is not English, may need materials adapted to their roles and reading needs, but the supplied evidence gives no basis for judging which formats reach them.
